### 🤖 Assistant: *Confirmed, and it is a real gap, though a…*

`16:48:24`

> Confirmed, and it is a real gap, though a narrow one. Here is the precise picture.
> 
> **What happens today.** A `Doorkeeper::AccessToken` created outside our model with no application, no `expires_in` and no scopes (the one-liner a console user, a plugin or a data migration would write) is, in the current branch:
> 
> - accessible forever: Doorkeeper's `expired?` is `!!(expires_in && ...)`, so nil means never expires;
> - full access: `full_access?` returns true, so `oauth_scope` is never set and the owner's complete rights apply, including admin;
> - tracked and listed: it appears on `my/api_tokens` with an empty name, an empty expiry cell and status "Active", and it can be revoked there.
> 
> I created exactly such a row for the admin in a rolled-back transaction and observed all three.
> 
> **What 6.1.2 did with the same row.** It authenticated but got `oauth_scope = []`, which makes `admin?` false and `allowed_to?` fail for everything. The row was a valid but useless credential. Our D-010 rule "application-less plus blank scopes equals full access" is what promotes it. So the branch changes the meaning of a data shape that already existed, and the promotion carries none of the PAT guarantees the ticket asks for: no mandatory expiry, no name, no last-four for identification.
> 
> **Why it is not a vulnerability.** Creating such a row requires the Rails console, a plugin, or direct database access. Anyone with those can already set the admin password, mint a legacy API key, or edit the OAuth tables directly, so no trust boundary is crossed. Doorkeeper's own flows always attach an application, so no HTTP path produces the row. The proper classification is a robustness and defensibility gap: a Redmine maintainer reading the MR will ask exactly your question, and the honest current answer is "yes, such a token becomes a never-ending full-access credential".
> 
> **Proposed fix: make the full-access test require the PAT invariant, not just the absence of an application.** One extra condition closes it:
> 
> ```ruby
> def self.full_access?(access_token)
>   access_token.application_id.nil? &&
>     access_token.expires_in.present? &&
>     access_token.scopes.all.empty?
> end
> ```
> 
> Effects:
> 
> - A genuine PAT always has `expires_in`, because the model derives it from the mandatory lifetime, so nothing changes for tokens created through the UI.
> - A foreign application-less token without expiry falls back to 6.1.2 behaviour: it authenticates with an empty scope and can do nothing. The "mandatory expiration" promise then holds for every full-access token in the table, whoever created it.
> - Fully backward compatible: no such token could do anything in 6.1.2 either.
> 
> A stricter variant also requires `name.present?`, which ties full access to "was created by our model". I would not go that far: `expires_in` is the property the ticket cares about, and requiring a name would punish a future admin tool that legitimately issues app-less tokens with expiry.
> 
> **Two companion changes.**
> 
> 1. A unit test in `personal_access_token_test.rb`, a fifth case in `test_full_access_should_be_true_only_for_app_less_token_with_blank_scopes`: an app-less token created with `expires_in: nil` is not full access. And an integration test: such a token on `/users.xml` for the admin gets 403, not 200.
> 2. README limits: "Tokens inserted into `oauth_access_tokens` outside the UI are not personal access tokens. Without an expiry they authenticate with no scope and can do nothing, as in 6.1.2. They do appear on the token page and can be revoked there."
> 
> Optionally, `scope :personal` and the `User#personal_access_tokens` association could also exclude rows without a name so the list only shows real PATs, but listing foreign rows is arguably useful, since it lets the owner see and revoke them. I would leave the listing as is and mention it.
> 
> **Process.** This changes spec 3.2's definition of `full_access?` and touches D-010's wording, so under D-026 it goes through a planner session: a `D-NNN` entry recording the gap, the chosen condition and the alternatives above, then the implementer applies it in step 4's files. I would treat it as recommended before the MR rather than optional: it costs three lines and two tests, and it turns a reviewer's question into a documented design property.
> 
> I will carry it as finding R-27 in the final whole-branch review.
